newsitem.title: SPAIN: Basques seek political unity against ETA violence.
newsitem.headline: Basques seek political unity against ETA violence.

text.p: Politicians in Spain's troubled Basque region agreed on Tuesday to try to form a united front against the separatist guerrilla group ETA, which has been blamed for four killings in the past week, regional officials said.

Against a backdrop of worsening violence in the guerrillas' long campaign, Basque region president Jose Antonio Ardanza summoned the signatories of a multi-party peace pact known as Ajuria Enea for talks on Friday.

"We're calling the meeting because at times like these when ETA is upsetting society, we want to send a message," Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) spokesman Inaki Anasagasti told reporters. "But ETA is not calling the meeting, we are."

The pact, originally signed nine years ago in the northern Spanish town of Ajuria Enea, gets representatives from all national and local parties together several times a year to try to produce a common position on thorny Basque nationalist issues.

Both Basque and central government officials believe the only way to stop ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom), which has killed around 800 people since starting an independence drive in 1968, is to mount a lucid, united voice for the Basque majority.

"The Basque society is disillusioned and dispirited," Spanish Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja told reporters after the funeral for the latest victim, a court guard who was killed when a bomb planted under his car exploded on Monday.
"There has to be unity among the political parties in the fight against terrorism."
Nationalist sentiment runs strong in the northern, industrial region, but only 15 percent of Basques approve of violence as a means to achieve more autonomy.
The last Ajuria Enea meeting fell apart in August because of severe differences among Basque politicians on a government decision to bury secret intelligence files on a 1980s "dirty war" against ETA.

The decision coincided with the controversial release without bail of a former Civil Guard commander on trial in one of the cases in the 1983-87 campaign of bombing, kidnappings, torture and murder of presumed ETA rebels.
Basque politicians have warned that there is still a lot of divided sentiment in the region and Friday's meeting could easily fail to reach a consensus.

"If the meeting tries to get all the parties to express a unanimous and energetic rejection of violence, that is guaranteed," Carlos Garaikoetxea, president of local nationalist party Eusko Alkartasuna, told reporters.
"But if it tries to set up a peace process overnight, I'm afraid that once again that's hoping for miracles."
Meanwhile, six more leaders of ETA's political wing Herri Batasuna (HB) were arrested on orders of the Supreme Court for failing to appear to answer charges they promoted violence.

The Supreme Court summonsed the entire 25-member HB leadership last month and since then 16 have been arrested, one hanged himself hours before his court date and three others went to Belgium to promote their cause.

HB has blamed the unrest in the region and ETA's recent wave of attacks -- the group is believed responsible for six assassinations this year including the shooting death of a Supreme Court judge -- on the jailings.
Some of the non-violent Basque politicians tend to sympathise with this argument and see the PNV, an ally of the ruling conservatives, as betraying the Basque people.
But politicians of all stripes agree the Ajuria Enea is vital for rebuilding a climate of peace in the region.
"We have to make a super-human effort to reconstruct the consensus that we have enjoyed the past few years," said top Basque interior ministry official Juan Maria Atutxa.
